sections.title: Bike-Share Schemes and Lost Property
sections.intro: Read the texts below and answer Questions 1–14.

paragraphs.text: One of the country's longest-running schemes, Calderbrook's CalderCycle uses docking stations, so every journey must start and finish at a station. Bikes are unlocked with the CalderCycle app. A single ride costs £1.50 for the first 30 minutes and £1 for every extra half-hour. An annual membership costs £90 and makes all rides under 45 minutes free, and full-time students pay just £45 for the same membership. If the station where you want to leave your bike is full, the app automatically gives you 15 extra minutes, free of charge, to reach another one. Riders must be 16 or over.

texts.label: B
texts.heading: Ostley Go
texts.subheading: 1,200 bikes; no docking stations; available 24 hours

paragraphs.text: Ostley Go is a dockless scheme, so instead of returning bikes to a station, riders can leave them in any of the marked parking bays on streets around the city. Anyone who leaves a bike outside the city's cycling zone, however, will be charged £25 to cover the cost of collecting it. Bikes are unlocked using the Ostley Go app, which also shows where every available bike is, and you can reserve one for up to ten minutes while you walk to it. Unlocking a bike costs 50p, and riding costs 10p a minute. About half the bikes are electric; these cost 20p a minute. Riders must be 18 or over.

texts.label: C
texts.heading: Penmarran Bike Hire
texts.subheading: 900 bikes; 85 docking stations; 6 am to midnight

paragraphs.text: Run by the city council, Penmarran Bike Hire is designed to link with the city's buses and trams. Bikes can be hired with a PenCard, the travel card used on all public transport in the city, or with a bank card at the touchscreen terminal at any docking station, so you do not need a smartphone. Hire is available from 6 am until midnight; after that, all bikes stay locked in their stations until the next morning. PenCard holders can ride for 30 minutes free of charge, and after that the cost is £1 per hour. Riders must be 16 or over.

Launched last year, E-Ride has a fleet made up entirely of electric bikes. The motor gives you extra power as you pedal, which makes Riverholm's steep hills much easier to climb, but it stops helping once you reach 15.5 mph. If the battery runs out during a journey, the bike can still be pedalled like an ordinary one. Bikes are hired through the E-Ride app and must be returned to a docking station; the cost is £1 plus 15p a minute. Young people aged 14 and 15 may use the scheme, as long as a parent or guardian has given permission through the app; all other riders must be 16 or over.

texts.heading: Fairholme Shopping Centre: Lost Property
texts.subheading: How to report a lost item and get it back

paragraphs.text: Items found in the centre's public areas, such as the walkways, toilets and food court, are taken to the Customer Service Desk on the ground floor, next to the Market Street entrance. If you think you left something in one of our shops, please contact the shop directly, as each store deals with its own lost property. The multi-storey car park is run by a separate company, Parkmoor, which should be contacted about anything lost there.

You can report a lost item at the Customer Service Desk, by phone or by completing the form on our website. Please describe the item in as much detail as possible, including its colour, size and any unusual features. You will be given a reference number, which you should quote whenever you contact us about the item. If a matching item is handed in, we will let you know by text message.

Most items are kept for 28 days, after which they are given to local charities. Because storage space is limited, however, umbrellas and clothing are kept for only 14 days. For security reasons, bank cards are destroyed as soon as they are handed in, so if your card is missing, please contact your bank immediately.

To collect an item, please bring your reference number and some photo identification, such as a passport or driving licence. If you cannot come yourself, a friend or relative may collect it for you, but they will need a signed letter from you as well as their own photo identification. Alternatively, small items can be posted to any UK address for £7.50.

questions.text: Riders can leave a bike somewhere other than a docking station.
questions.explanation: Ostley Go is dockless: riders "can leave them in any of the marked parking bays". The other three schemes all use docking stations.

questions.text: Students are offered a cheaper membership.
questions.explanation: Full-time students "pay just £45 for the same membership", which costs others £90. Penmarran's free 30 minutes (C) is for all PenCard holders, not students.

questions.text: A smartphone is not needed to hire a bike.
questions.explanation: Penmarran bikes can be hired with a PenCard or a bank card, "so you do not need a smartphone". Schemes A, B and D all require an app.

questions.text: Every bike has an electric motor.
questions.explanation: E-Ride "has a fleet made up entirely of electric bikes". At Ostley Go (B), only about half the bikes are electric.

questions.text: Riders are given extra time at no cost if they cannot leave a bike where they intended to.
questions.explanation: If a station is full, the CalderCycle app "gives you 15 extra minutes, free of charge". Penmarran's free 30 minutes (C) applies to every PenCard ride.

questions.text: Bikes cannot be hired late at night.
questions.explanation: Penmarran hire runs "from 6 am until midnight", and bikes stay locked until the morning. Schemes A, B and D are available 24 hours.

questions.text: Riders can reserve a bike before they reach it.
questions.explanation: With the Ostley Go app, "you can reserve one for up to ten minutes" while walking to it. No other scheme mentions reserving.

questions.text: Some riders under the age of 16 are allowed to use the scheme.
questions.explanation: E-Ride lets "Young people aged 14 and 15" ride with a parent's permission. The other schemes require riders to be 16 or 18 or over.

sections.title: Workplace and Careers Guidance
sections.intro: Read the texts below and answer Questions 15–27.

texts.heading: Fire safety in the office
texts.subheading: Guidance for all staff at Carrick House

paragraphs.text: Fires in offices are rare, but when they do start, they can spread very quickly. All staff at Carrick House are expected to follow the guidance below, and new employees must complete the online fire safety course during their first month. Every floor has two trained fire wardens, whose names are displayed next to the lifts.

Preventing fires: Electrical faults are one of the most common causes of office fires. Do not bring personal electrical items, such as heaters or fans, into the building unless they have been checked by the facilities team. Never plug one extension lead into another, and report any damaged cables immediately. Fire doors slow the spread of smoke and flames, so they must never be propped open, even on hot days.

Alarm tests: The fire alarm is tested every Wednesday at 10 am. During the test, the alarm sounds for less than a minute and you do not need to leave the building. If the alarm sounds at any other time, or for longer than a minute, leave immediately. Fire drills are held twice a year without warning.

If you discover a fire: Raise the alarm by pressing the nearest call point; these red boxes are found beside every exit. Only try to put out a fire if it is small and you have been trained to use an extinguisher. Never use water on an electrical fire: use the extinguisher with a black label, which contains carbon dioxide.

Leaving the building: Use the nearest safe exit and close doors behind you. Do not use the lifts, and do not stop to collect your belongings. Go straight to the assembly point in the staff car park and report to your fire warden, who will check that everyone is safe. Do not go back inside until the fire service says it is safe to do so.

texts.heading: Writing a strong job application
texts.subheading: Advice from the Corran College Careers Service

paragraphs.text: Employers often receive hundreds of applications for a single job, and many spend less than a minute on each one before deciding whether to read on. Your application therefore needs to show quickly and clearly why you are a good match for the role.

Before you start writing, study the job description and the person specification. The person specification sets out the skills and qualities the employer is looking for, and these are usually divided into 'essential' and 'desirable' criteria. Your application should provide evidence for every essential criterion; if it does not, it is unlikely to be shortlisted. It is also worth reading the organisation's website, so that you can explain why you want to work there in particular.

Your CV should normally be no longer than two pages, with your education and work experience listed in reverse chronological order, starting with the most recent. Rather than simply listing your duties, describe what you achieved, using figures where possible: 'increased online sales by 15%' is far more convincing than 'responsible for online sales'. Adapt your CV for each job rather than sending the same version to every employer.

Unless the advertisement says otherwise, always send a covering letter with your CV. Try to find out the name of the person who will read it, rather than writing 'Dear Sir or Madam', and keep it to a single page.

Spelling mistakes can cost you an interview, and spell-checkers will not notice if you type 'manger' instead of 'manager', so ask a friend to read your application too. If you are completing an online form, write your answers in a separate document first, as some systems log you out after a period of inactivity and your work may be lost. Finally, keep a copy of everything you send, because you may be asked about it at interview.
The Careers Service offers free 20-minute appointments to review applications. Please book through the student portal at least three working days before your deadline.

sections.title: Cool Without Electricity
sections.intro: Read the text below and answer Questions 28–40.

texts.heading: Cool Without Electricity
texts.subheading: What traditional desert buildings can teach today's architects

paragraphs.text: On a summer afternoon in the deserts of the Middle East or North Africa, the temperature outside can climb above 45°C. Step inside an old house built of mud brick, however, and the air may feel surprisingly comfortable, even though there is no air conditioner in sight. Over many centuries, builders in hot, dry regions developed ways of keeping buildings cool using little more than shade, moving air and water. Many of these methods fell out of use in the twentieth century, when air conditioning and cheap electricity made them seem old-fashioned. Now, as global demand for cooling rises rapidly and air-conditioning units pump yet more heat into crowded city streets, a growing number of architects are looking again at what traditional builders knew.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The most striking of these techniques is the wind tower, or wind catcher, which can still be seen rising above the rooftops in parts of Iran, the Gulf and Egypt. A wind tower is a tall, hollow structure with openings near the top. Because the wind blows more strongly and carries less dust high above the ground, the openings catch breezes that hardly reach the narrow streets below. This moving air is channelled down a shaft into the rooms beneath, while warmer air inside the house is pushed out through windows or through openings on the sheltered side of the tower. Even on a completely still day, the tower is not useless: as the sun heats it, the air inside it warms and rises out of the top, drawing air through the house behind it.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Water made these systems even more effective. In some houses, air coming down a wind tower passed over a pool or an underground water channel before entering the living areas. In others, porous clay jars filled with water were placed in the path of the breeze. In both cases, some of the water evaporated, and because evaporation absorbs heat from the surrounding air, the breeze was noticeably cooler by the time it reached the people inside. Fountains and shallow pools in courtyards worked in the same way. The method has one important limitation, however: it works well only when the air is dry. In humid coastal areas, where the air already holds a great deal of moisture, far less water evaporates and the cooling effect is much weaker.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Builders also made clever use of heavy materials. The walls of desert houses were often half a metre or more thick and were made of mud brick or stone. Walls like these do not keep heat out completely, but they absorb it slowly, so the heat of the midday sun may take many hours to pass through them. By the time it reaches the rooms inside, it is evening, and the stored heat can escape into the much cooler night air. In some areas, outside walls were whitewashed to reflect sunlight, and windows facing the street were usually kept small. Larger openings were frequently covered with wooden lattice screens, which blocked the direct rays of the sun while still allowing air to pass through.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Many traditional homes were built around a central courtyard, with rooms opening onto it rather than onto the street. At night, cool air sinks into the courtyard and collects there, and the surrounding walls keep it shaded for much of the following day. Families often moved around the house according to the time of day and the season, sleeping on the roof on summer nights and retreating to cooler ground-floor rooms in the heat of the afternoon. Whole neighbourhoods were planned in a similar spirit. Houses were built close together along narrow, winding streets, so that buildings shaded one another as well as the streets between them.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Today, architects are finding new ways to apply these ideas. Dalia Rostami, who designs schools in hot, dry regions, recently completed a primary school whose classrooms are arranged around two shaded courtyards and ventilated by a pair of wind towers. For most of the year, the classrooms stay comfortable without air conditioning, and on the hottest days, small fans powered by solar panels help to pull air through the towers. The school's energy bills are a fraction of those of similar schools nearby. Meanwhile, the engineer Karim Bensaid uses computer models to predict how air will move through a building before it is built. 'Traditional builders perfected their designs over generations of trial and error,' he says. 'We can test a hundred versions of a wind tower in an afternoon.' Neither of them believes that such techniques can replace air conditioning entirely, especially in tall buildings or humid cities. 'The aim is not to go back in time,' says Rostami. 'It is to let the building do most of the work, so that machines are only needed for what is left.'
paragraphs.label: F
